failures.title: BMW S58B30T Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Crankshaft Bearing Quality Issues (2021 production)
items.whatHappens: In 2021, BMW identified a quality control problem with supplied main bearing shells on the S58B30T0. Multiple engines were found with defective bearings during quality checks, forcing BMW to temporarily halt M3 and M4 deliveries until the issue was resolved. The problem affected a specific batch of engines and was addressed under warranty.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught during production or pre-delivery, bearing replacement was the fix. If the engine has already suffered bearing failure (scored crank, seized engine), a full replacement is required - this is catastrophic and writes off the unit.

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - radiators, hoses, expansion tank
items.whatHappens: The S58 runs hot - it's a 500+ hp twin-turbo engine in a tightly packed engine bay. Common failures include cracked expansion tanks, degraded coolant hoses, and radiator leaks. Coolant loss can lead to rapid overheating and head gasket failure if not addressed.
items.repairVsReplace: Cooling system components are individually replaceable - this is a maintenance item, not an engine-killer, provided it's caught before overheating occurs. Preventative replacement of hoses and expansion tank at 50k miles is strongly recommended.

items.title: Oil Consumption - valve stem seals
items.whatHappens: The S58B30T can consume oil through worn valve stem seals, particularly on cars that have been tracked or driven hard. Symptoms include blue smoke on start-up and between oil changes requiring top-ups.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a labour-intensive but standalone repair (cylinder head-off job). If oil consumption is ignored, it can lead to carbon buildup, clogged catalysts, and eventually engine damage.

failures.goodYearsLine: The S58B30T is generally considered robust, but 2021 production cars with the crank bearing issue should be checked for recall completion. Post-2022 units are significantly more reliable, with the bearing problem resolved and cooling system revisions introduced.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the S58B30T
variants.intro: The S58B30T (also designated S58B30T0) is BMW's high-output Competition-spec S58 engine, produced from 2019 to the present. It is distinguished from the base S58B30O0 by higher boost pressure, revised engine mapping, and pairing exclusively with the 8-speed M Steptronic automatic transmission. Where to find the engine code: - On the engine block - a stamped plate near the front left (viewed from the driver's seat) - On the V5C registration document - under engine number - Via a BMW VIN decoder - the 7th and 8th characters of the VIN identify the engine family Commonly confused codes: - S58B30O0 - the base S58 variant (473 hp), paired with the 6-speed manual transmission in M3/M4 - S58B30T0 - the Competition variant (510-530 hp), paired with the 8-speed automatic - S58B30O1 - later S58 variant used in some M2 models - S58TU2 - future S58 update with revised hardware【LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory】

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S58B30T - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S58B30T makes sense only with full provenance - documented service history, proof of no track abuse, and confirmation that any 2021 bearing recall work has been completed. A used unit from a written-off M car can be a cost-effective option (£4,500-£6,500), but the risk is high: these engines are often pushed hard. Only buy with a compression test and borescope inspection. Used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper S58B30T recon addresses the engine's specific weak points: new cooling system components (water pump, expansion tank, hoses), valve stem seals, and a full inspection of the bottom end (bearings, crank). This is the right call for most S58B30T owners - the engine is fundamentally strong, and addressing the known failure points gives a reliable unit with 12-24 months warranty. Expect to pay £5,200-£8,500. Reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full S58B30T rebuild is justified for high-performance applications - track cars, heavily tuned examples, or CS/CSL owners who want to ensure absolute reliability. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded rod bearings, improved cooling system components, and a thorough blueprint of the closed-deck block. This is the premium option at £7,500-£11,000. Rebuilt engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All our vetted UK BMW M specialists offer supply-only or full supply-and-fit - 12-month warranty on reconditioned units, nationwide delivery available. Supply and fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The S58B30T sits in BMW M cars worth £25,000-£80,000+ depending on age and mileage. A reconditioned S58B30T at £5,200-£8,500 represents 10-30% of vehicle value - comfortably viable for most hosts. However, for a high-mileage F97 X3 M worth under £25,000, a used unit (£4,500-£6,500) may be the more financially sensible choice. Always evaluate your vehicle's condition and value before committing to a reconditioned unit.

mainEntity.name: How much does an S58B30T engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned S58B30T supply‑only typically costs £5,200-£8,500, with fitted prices ranging from £5,950 to £9,660 depending on labour and parts. Used units are cheaper at £4,500-£6,500 but carry higher risk. Rebuilt units cost £7,500-£11,000. Warranty is typically 12-24 months on reconditioned/rebuilt units.

mainEntity.name: What are the common problems with the S58B30T engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most documented failures are cooling system leaks (expansion tank, hoses) and a batch of 2021 crank bearing quality issues. Cooling system leaks can lead to rapid overheating if not addressed. 2021 bearing issues were addressed under recall; check completion. Oil consumption through valve stem seals can occur on tracked cars.

mainEntity.name: Which BMW M models have the S58B30T engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The S58B30T powers M3 Competition (G80), M4 Competition (G82/G83), X3 M Competition (F97), X4 M Competition (F98), M3 CS, M4 CSL, and M3 Touring (G81) from 2019 onwards. It is the Competition‑spec variant, paired exclusively with the 8‑speed automatic. Base M3/M4 with manual transmission use the lower‑output S58B30O0.

mainEntity.name: Should I buy a used or reconditioned S58B30T?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned S58B30T is the safer choice because it addresses the engine's known weak points (cooling system, seals, bearings) and comes with a warranty. Used units are cheaper but risk carrying unaddressed issues or track abuse. For high‑mileage M cars worth under £25,000, a used engine may be more cost‑effective.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my car has the S58B30T and not another S58 variant?

acceptedAnswer.text: The engine code is stamped on the block (front left side) and listed on your V5C or via a BMW VIN decoder. It is commonly confused with S58B30O0 (base, manual) and S58B30O1 (later variant). The S58B30T is the Competition variant with higher boost and automatic transmission only.

mainEntity.name: Is the S58B30T a reliable engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Overall, the S58 is BMW's most advanced inline‑six, and the S58B30T is robust when maintained properly. 2021 bearing recall aside, the engine is track‑tested and durable. Preventative cooling system maintenance at 50k miles is recommended. The closed‑deck block and forged internals support high power safely.
